motivation: To understand the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome ice compound HoAgGe, which exhibits spin ice behavior and potential hidden order.
method: Nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements combined with neutron scattering and other techniques to probe the magnetic phase transition and symmetry breaking.
result: The system undergoes a three-dimensional XY universality class transition, and the ground state shows hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking.
conclusion: The study provides evidence for a novel magnetic ground state in kagome ice systems, relevant to frustrated magnetism and phase transitions.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature, characterized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but many are only stable at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature platform for studying such states.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to measure the electronic band structure, revealing flat bands that persist at room temperature.
result: Intrinsic orbital-selective flat bands are observed that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.
conclusion: These materials offer a promising system for exploring flat-band physics and potentially correlated phenomena at accessible temperatures.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall States In Twisted Bilayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ Via Attractive Polaron Spectroscopy
authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi
abstract:
Author(s): Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, and Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021037] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses magneto-optical spectroscopy to probe quantum anomalous Hall states in twisted bilayer WSe2, demonstrating electric-field control of magnetic order.
motivation: To investigate the quantum anomalous Hall phase in twisted bilayer WSe2 and understand the interplay between topology and magnetism in moiré materials.
method: The authors perform magneto-optical spectroscopy, specifically attractive polaron spectroscopy, on twisted bilayer WSe2 devices under applied electric and magnetic fields.
result: They observe a spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase and demonstrate electric-field control over transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders.
conclusion: The work establishes twisted bilayer WSe2 as a platform for studying quantum anomalous Hall states and electrically tunable magnetism.

title: Liquid-Gas Criticality Of Hyperuniform Fluids
authors: Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, And Qun-Li Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, and Qun-Li Lei

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021032] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, a topic in soft condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand the unusual behavior of hyperuniform fluids at the liquid-vapor critical point, where fluctuations are suppressed yet susceptibility is high.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and possibly simulations to investigate the critical properties of hyperuniform fluids composed of spinning particles.
result: They find that hyperuniform fluids exhibit suppressed density fluctuations but enhanced susceptibility at the critical point, deviating from ordinary fluids.
conclusion: Hyperuniform fluids present a new class of critical behavior with potential implications for materials design.

title: Ballistic Spin Valve In Graphene Realized Via Electron Optics
authors: Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, And Ivan J. Vera-Marun
abstract:
Author(s): Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, and Ivan J. Vera-Marun

Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene reveals gate-tunable ballistic spin transport, providing a mechanism for coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021029] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a ballistic spin valve in graphene using transverse magnetic focusing, enabling gate-tunable spin transport via electron optics.
motivation: To achieve coherent spin control in graphene for spintronic applications by leveraging ballistic transport and electron optics.
method: Encapsulated graphene devices are used to perform transverse magnetic focusing, revealing spin-dependent electron trajectories.
result: Gate-tunable ballistic spin transport is observed, demonstrating a spin valve effect based on spin-dependent electron optics.
conclusion: The work provides a mechanism for coherent spin control in graphene, advancing spintronics and electron optics.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, focusing on condensed matter physics without connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex ordering; understanding the nematic state may clarify their behavior.
method: The authors likely use experimental or theoretical methods to characterize the dipolar nematic phase.
result: They identify a dipolar nematic state and describe its properties.
conclusion: The nematic ordering is key to relaxor ferroelectric behavior.

title: Excitations Across The Equilibrium And Photoinduced “Hidden” States Of Magnetoresistive Manganites
authors: Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, And Jonathan Pelliciari
abstract:
Author(s): Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, and Jonathan Pelliciari

Ultrafast photoexcitation in /3Ca1/3MnO3 generates a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations that do not exist under standard equilibrium conditions.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021018] Published Thu Apr 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies photoinduced hidden phases and excitations in magnetoresistive manganites using ultrafast spectroscopy and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering.
motivation: To understand the nature of photoinduced hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems, which may have implications for controlling material properties.
method: Combined ultrafast optical pump-probe spectroscopy and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to probe excitations across equilibrium and hidden states.
result: Discovery of unique polaronic and phononic excitations in the hidden phase that are absent in equilibrium, indicating a distinct electronic and lattice configuration.
conclusion: Photoexcitation can stabilize a long-lived hidden phase with novel excitations, offering a pathway to manipulate correlated materials.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a powerful tool for extracting features from data, but classical algorithms are computationally expensive. Quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and sampling techniques to compute persistence diagrams.
result: They prove a provable exponential speedup over classical algorithms for certain classes of inputs.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a potential practical application of quantum computing in data analysis, though practical implementation remains challenging.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A high-level perspective piece proposing a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, focusing on scientific milestones rather than technical results.
motivation: To outline a roadmap bridging the gap between current quantum computing capabilities and real-world applications.
method: Conceptual framework based on expert opinion and analysis of the field's progress.
result: A five-stage framework detailing milestones for quantum utility.
conclusion: The framework provides a structured path but does not present new technical contributions.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithms For The Jones Polynomial
authors: Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew Decross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, And Konstantinos Meichanetzidis
abstract:
Author(s): Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew DeCross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, and Konstantinos Meichanetzidis

A comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial is shown to serve as a benchmark for quantum computers and yield new insights into potential quantum advantage.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, serving as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a topological invariant that is hard to compute classically, making it a candidate for quantum advantage. The authors aim to demonstrate an end-to-end quantum algorithm that can be run on current hardware.
method: The paper describes a complete pipeline including state preparation, unitary evolution, and measurement, implemented on a trapped-ion quantum processor. It uses a Hadamard test and ancilla qubits to estimate the Jones polynomial.
result: The algorithm successfully approximates the Jones polynomial for small knots, showing agreement with classical calculations and demonstrating the feasibility of the approach.
conclusion: The work provides a practical benchmark for quantum computers and suggests that the Jones polynomial is a promising candidate for demonstrating quantum advantage in the near term.

title: Photon Catalysis For General Multimode Multi-Photon Quantum State Preparation
authors: Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, And Massimo Frigerio
abstract:
Author(s): Andrei Aralov, Émilie Gillet, Viet Nguyen, Andrea Cosentino, Mattia Walschaers, and Massimo Frigerio

Using a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition, every photonic state can be prepared with realistic experimental tools and a predictable number of steps.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020323] Published Wed May 06, 2026.
tldr: A method for preparing arbitrary photonic states using symmetric tensor decomposition and photon catalysis.
motivation: Efficient preparation of complex photonic states is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are often limited to specific states or require many resources.
method: The authors propose a procedure based on symmetric tensor decomposition to decompose any target photonic state into a sequence of photon catalysis operations, which are experimentally feasible with current technology.
result: They show that any multimode multi-photon state can be prepared with a predictable number of steps using realistic experimental tools.
conclusion: The work provides a general and scalable framework for photonic state preparation, potentially enabling new quantum information protocols.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025005] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, focusing on HHL and post-HHL developments.
motivation: Linear system solving is a central task in computation, and quantum algorithms promise exponential speedups for certain problems.
method: The paper reviews algorithmic techniques including HHL, block-encoding, quantum signal processing, and variable-time amplitude amplification.
result: It catalogs the evolution of quantum linear system solvers, highlighting improvements in query complexity, condition number dependence, and error scaling.
conclusion: Quantum linear system solvers have matured significantly, but practical implementation remains challenging due to resource requirements and noise.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge in 2D magnetism, which has seen rapid progress since 2016.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical results on 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: Covers ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and multiferroics.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated and topological electronic states, with implications for future quantum materials.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with broad applications to physical systems.
motivation: Spin glasses are a paradigmatic model for complex systems, and understanding their dynamics is crucial for many areas of physics.
method: The paper reviews experimental techniques, theoretical approaches (e.g., mean-field theory, replica method), and large-scale numerical simulations.
result: It highlights the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation in advancing the field, and identifies open questions.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remains an active area with opportunities for future research, but the paper does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on material candidates and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: The paper reviews theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in candidate materials, discussing their magnetic properties and topological features.
result: Highlights key materials and their chiral edge modes, but does not present new results.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain an active area of research with many open questions, and the review serves as a guide for future work.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to neural network data, but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a central problem in neuroscience, and statistical physics offers powerful tools for modeling such systems.
method: The authors review recent progress in using maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques to analyze recordings from thousands of neurons simultaneously.
result: These methods uncover reproducible collective behaviors in neural populations, demonstrating that abstract theoretical principles from physics can have predictive power in neuroscience.
conclusion: Statistical mechanics provides a quantitative bridge between neural data and theory, revealing emergent properties of neural networks.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: A colloquium review of quantum aspects of magnetic skyrmions, covering their formation and quantum features.
motivation: To survey quantum-mechanical properties of skyrmions, which are topological spin textures with potential applications in spintronics.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion quantum interactions and quantum features.
result: Summarizes current understanding of quantum effects in skyrmions, including quantum tunneling and entanglement.
conclusion: Quantum properties of skyrmions are an emerging area with potential for future quantum technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of quantum many-body systems in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions, focusing on simulating condensed matter and gravity phenomena.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries that are difficult to realize in natural materials, enabling simulation of topological phases and gravitational models.
method: The paper surveys platforms such as ultracold atoms, photonic systems, and electronic materials, discussing how to engineer fractal lattices, synthetic dimensions, and curved spaces.
result: It summarizes key experimental achievements and theoretical proposals for realizing synthetic quantum matter in these geometries, highlighting connections to topology and gravity.
conclusion: Synthetic quantum matter in nonstandard geometries is a rapidly advancing field with potential to uncover new physics, but it remains largely exploratory and not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of using massive quantum systems to probe gravity, including tests of quantum gravity effects and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is poorly tested at quantum scales; massive quantum systems may reveal quantum aspects of gravity.
method: Reviews theoretical proposals and experimental efforts to detect gravity-induced decoherence, collapse, and entanglement.
result: Summarizes current state-of-the-art experiments and theoretical models for testing gravity with quantum probes.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems can serve as interfaces to study gravity, but no definitive results yet; further experiments needed.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library for modular optical layout and demonstrates its use for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in AMO experiments is not scalable due to piecewise setup; a modular, code-to-CAD approach is needed.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a Python library with beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, and creates modular baseplates for laser subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D-printed baseplates.
conclusion: The modular approach enables scalable optical systems for quantum computing and fosters open-source collaborative hardware design.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) and variable bosonic excitations, applied to a benchmark lithium wave function.
result: The wave function is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: This compact characterization reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Classical Field Simulation Of Vortex Lattice Melting In A Two-dimensional Fast Rotating Bose Gas
authors: Sálvio J Bereta, Lucas Madeira, Mônica A Caracanhas, Hélène Perrin And Romain Dubessy
abstract: We present a classical field simulation study of the thermal melting of a two-dimensional (2D) vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on the role of finite-size effects on the melting temperature. This work constitutes a numerical continuation of the recent experimental investigation reported in (Sharma 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett.133 143401), which addressed the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a quasi-2D Bose gas. Using the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap, we simulate the finite-temperature equilibrium state and extract vortex configurations from density snapshots. Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified. Our simulations enable a detailed characterization of the crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases through correlation functions quantifying the translational and orientational order and through defect statistics. Finite-size effects are shown to play a crucial role at lower rotation frequencies, affecting the proliferation of lattice defects.
tldr: Classical field simulation of vortex lattice melting in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on finite-size effects and the KTHNY melting scenario.
motivation: To numerically study the thermal melting of a 2D vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, complementing recent experiments and clarifying the role of finite-size effects.
method: Uses the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap to simulate finite-temperature equilibrium states, extracting vortex configurations from density snapshots.
result: Clear signatures of two-step KTHNY melting are observed; finite-size effects significantly affect defect proliferation at lower rotation frequencies.
conclusion: The simulations confirm the KTHNY melting scenario and highlight the importance of finite-size effects in interpreting experimental data.

title: Direct Derivation Of The Modified Langevin Noise Formalism From The Canonical Quantization Of Macroscopic Electromagnetism
authors: A Ciattoni
abstract: The modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) models the interaction of the quantized electromagnetic field with an arbitrary lossy magneto-dielectric object placed in vacuum using three types of non-interacting bosonic polaritons: scattering, electric, and magnetic. These respectively represent free-space photons scattered by the object, and photons radiated by quantized electric and magnetic dipolar sources embedded within its volume. Recently (Ciattoni 2024 Phys. Rev. A110 013707), this formalism was justified from the canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) (Philbin 2010 New J. Phys.12 123008) in the Heisenberg picture. This was achieved by identifying the polariton operators within the formal solution of the macroscopic Maxwell equations, assuming they obey bosonic commutation relations to retrieve the canonical ones, and showing they diagonalize the CQME Hamiltonian. However, the explicit functional dependence of these polaritons on the underlying canonical field operators remained undetermined. In this paper, we derive the exact analytical expressions for the polariton operators in terms of the canonical CQME field operators. Using these mappings, we provide a direct and rigorous derivation of the MLNF from the canonical theory in the Schrödinger picture. Our derivation is structured in three foundational steps: 1) adopting the derived analytical expressions as the constitutive definitions of the polariton operators; 2) mathematically proving that these operators are strictly bosonic as a direct consequence of the canonical commutation relations; and 3) demonstrating that they exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian.
tldr: This paper derives explicit analytical expressions for polariton operators in the modified Langevin noise formalism from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism.
motivation: To provide a rigorous derivation of the modified Langevin noise formalism (MLNF) from canonical quantization of macroscopic electromagnetism (CQME) by finding explicit mappings between polariton operators and canonical field operators.
method: The authors derive exact analytical expressions for scattering, electric, and magnetic polariton operators in terms of canonical CQME field operators, then prove they satisfy bosonic commutation relations and diagonalize the Hamiltonian.
result: The polariton operators are shown to be strictly bosonic and exactly diagonalize the macroscopic CQME Hamiltonian, providing a direct derivation of MLNF in the Schrödinger picture.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous foundation for MLNF, confirming its consistency with canonical quantization and enabling further applications in quantum optics with lossy media.

title: A Frequency-domain Identifiability Law For Deterministic Reconstruction Of Complex Networks Under Partial Observability
authors: Tianlong Fan And Linyuan Lü Xiaoxiao Liang
abstract: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral observations is central to computational studies of complex systems, with implications for detecting covert actors in terrorist networks, localizing unobserved brain regions, and revealing latent molecular regulators. Focusing on evolutionary game dynamics, we uncover an empirically consistent frequency-domain regularity: the aggregated magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a node’s payoff time series scales linearly with its structural degree, , across tested topologies and parameter regimes. Leveraging this structure–behavior scaling, we develop a deterministic inference framework that (i) estimates degrees directly from DFT spectra via a single global-slope fit, and (ii) uses brief, identifiability-oriented local interventions (‘suppress-and-measure’) to reveal adjacencies through intervention-induced spectral drops. Discrepancies between estimated degree and revealed neighbors deterministically enumerate external edges to hidden components and yield tight lower/upper bounds on the number of unobserved nodes. We analyze the conditions under which the scaling holds, quantify deviations under structural heterogeneity, and characterize sample-length dependence. Experiments on synthetic and empirical networks demonstrate accurate topology recovery, robustness to stochasticity, and scalability to thousand-node graphs, with consistent gains over causality-, correlation-, information-, and likelihood-based baselines. These results establish a DFT-based route to structure discovery under partial observability, translating local spectral measurements into actionable structural information.
tldr: This paper uses DFT of payoff time series to infer network structure from partial observations in evolutionary game dynamics.
motivation: Inferring network architecture from partial behavioral data is important for detecting hidden actors in various complex systems.
method: The authors discover a linear scaling between DFT magnitude of payoff time series and node degree, then use a suppress-and-measure intervention to identify adjacencies.
result: The method accurately recovers network topology, outperforms baselines, and provides bounds on unobserved nodes.
conclusion: DFT-based spectral measurements can effectively reveal network structure under partial observability.

title: Strong Field Ionized Electron Trajectories Driven By Squeezed Light
authors: Alex Schimmoller And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: In atomic strong field ionization, a photoelectron’s motion is largely determined by the laser pulse’s expected electric field, as well as the atomic potential. However, when the ionization is performed by squeezed light, the photon’s quantum statistics can modify these dynamics. In this work, we generalize the classical trajectory Monte–Carlo technique to study strong field ionization by squeezed states of light. We find that electrons driven by phase-squeezed pulses exhibit increases in longitudinal momentum consistent with what is expected from the field statistics. Meanwhile, the transverse momentum distribution shows varying influence of ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ rescattering off the Coulomb potential, and the proportion of electrons recaptured as Rydberg states decreases monotonically with the amount of squeezed light applied. This work demonstrates the added experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics achievable by tuning light’s quantum statistics, as well as the essential role of the atomic potential in strong field ionization.
tldr: This paper studies the effect of squeezed light on electron trajectories in strong field ionization, showing that quantum statistics of light can modify electron dynamics.
motivation: To understand how the quantum statistics of light, specifically squeezed states, affect strong field ionization and electron dynamics beyond classical field descriptions.
method: Generalized classical trajectory Monte-Carlo technique to simulate strong field ionization by squeezed states of light, incorporating the atomic potential.
result: Phase-squeezed pulses increase longitudinal momentum; transverse momentum distribution shows varying rescattering effects; Rydberg recapture decreases with squeezing.
conclusion: Squeezed light offers additional experimental control over ultrafast electron dynamics, and the atomic potential plays a crucial role in these processes.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which had not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable vortex solitons.
result: They discover two classes of stable vortex solitons with in-phase or out-of-phase bright spots, and find that low-charge vortex solitons can be stable, with stability intervals broadening as rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic potential landscape in graphene devices is crucial for engineering advanced 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
method: In operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution is used to image the valence band edge across a graphene device under bias and gate voltage.
result: The electric field in graphene covered with AlOx and TiOx is suppressed by up to 50% compared to bare graphene, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to uncover potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D devices.

method: The authors introduce a 'random-with-constraints' framework that generates minimal models by imposing random constraints on high-dimensional data.
result: The approach yields interpretable models that capture essential dynamics while remaining tractable.
conclusion: The method provides a principled way to build minimal models for high-dimensional biological systems, bridging data-driven and theory-driven approaches.

title: Causality Of Ultrafast Photoionization From Argon 3 S Usin...
authors: Rezvan Tahouri And Jan Marcus Dahlström
abstract: We study real-time photoionization flux at the Amusia–Cooper minimum (ACM) in argon using ab initio simulations with the relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) method in length (LG) and velocity (VG) gauges. A simple analytical model is used to interpret the results, and to construct Wigner delays and Wigner distributions for both gauges and relativistic channels of the photoelectron ( with and ). The two gauges are found to produce qualitatively different ionization dynamics, with LG having positive and VG having negative Wigner delays. The advancement of several femtoseconds, found for Wigner delays in VG, raises some concern for causality when atoms are ionized by attosecond pulses that are shorter than the absolute value of the Wigner delay. Reassuringly, numerical simulations of wave packets with RTDCIS show that the electrons behave in a causal way in both gauges. Weighted delays that take into account the temporal window of excitation (or the bandwidth of the pulses) are constructed from the Wigner distribution to reach agreement between the numerical simulations and our simple wave packet model. Furthermore, a strong effect of spin–orbit coupling of the photoelectron ( ) is reported for ultrafast photoionization dynamics, and Schrödinger kitten and cat states are identified in the Wigner distributions as a result of the ACM. Our work paves the way for a deeper understanding of ultrafast photoionization and the role of causality in systems with strong electron–electron correlation effects.
tldr: This paper studies ultrafast photoionization dynamics in argon, focusing on causality and Wigner delays at the Amusia-Cooper minimum.
motivation: To understand real-time photoionization flux and causality in attosecond pulses, especially when Wigner delays exceed pulse duration.
method: Ab initio simulations using relativistic time-dependent configuration-interaction singles (RTDCIS) in length and velocity gauges, combined with a simple analytical model.
result: Length and velocity gauges yield qualitatively different Wigner delays (positive vs negative), but numerical simulations confirm causal behavior in both gauges; spin-orbit coupling and Schrödinger cat states are observed.
conclusion: The work provides deeper insight into ultrafast photoionization and causality in strongly correlated systems.

title: Photon Accelerator In Magnetized Electron–ion Plasma
authors: S V Bulanov, S S Bulanov, T Z Esirkepov, G Gregori, G M Grittani, M Lamač, B K Russell, A G R Thomas And P Valenta
abstract: Strong magnetic fields and plasmas are intrinsically linked in both terrestrial laboratory experiments and in space phenomena. One of the most profound consequences of that is the change in relationship between the frequency and the wave number of electromagnetic waves propagating in plasma in the presence of such magnetic fields when compared to the case without these fields. Furthermore, magnetic fields alter electromagnetic wave interaction with relativistic plasma waves, resulting in different outcomes for particle and radiation generation. For a relativistic plasma wave-based photon acceleration this leads to an increased frequency gain and, thus, potentially to higher efficiency. The influence of a magnetic field leads to quantitative and qualitative change in the properties of photon acceleration, amplifying the increase in the electromagnetic wave frequency.
tldr: This paper studies photon acceleration in magnetized electron-ion plasma, focusing on frequency upshifts due to magnetic fields.
motivation: To understand how strong magnetic fields alter electromagnetic wave propagation and photon acceleration in plasma, with potential applications in high-energy radiation sources.
method: Theoretical analysis using relativistic plasma wave models and magnetohydrodynamics to derive frequency shifts and acceleration efficiency.
result: Magnetic fields enhance the frequency gain of photons during acceleration, leading to higher efficiency compared to unmagnetized cases.
conclusion: Magnetized plasma can improve photon acceleration, offering a path to more efficient generation of high-frequency electromagnetic waves.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in a triangular-lattice antiferromagnet, focusing on magnetoelastic coupling and Fermi surface nesting.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic orders in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, possibly due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for analyzing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden defect extension of 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel double-particle operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

Single-ion optical clocks have shown systematic frequency uncertainties below [MATH], but typically require more than one week of averaging to achieve a corresponding statistical uncertainty. This time can be reduced with longer probe times, but comes at the cost of a higher time-dilation shif…

tldr: This paper presents a high-stability optical clock based on a single Al+ ion with continuous ground-state cooling, achieving reduced averaging time without compromising accuracy.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: A multi-step process involving surface defects, electrical stress, heating, and particle emission is identified as the trigger for vacuum arcs.
conclusion: Improved understanding can guide the design of more robust accelerator structures and other high-power technologies.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: A review of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on wave-matter interactions and particle manipulation.
motivation: To provide a unified perspective on how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in wave fields induce forces and torques on particles.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on optical and acoustic radiation forces, including trapping, sorting, and pulling effects.
result: Summarizes key mechanisms and applications of radiation forces and torques in both optics and acoustics.
conclusion: The field has broad applications in particle manipulation, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: A colloquium on multimessenger astronomy with continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and future detectors.
motivation: To discuss detection prospects and astrophysical implications of continuous gravitational waves, linking to electromagnetic observations and dense matter physics.
method: Review of current and future gravitational-wave detectors, and multimessenger observation strategies.
result: Highlights the potential for multimessenger observations to probe neutron star interiors and nuclear astrophysics.
conclusion: Continuous gravitational waves offer a new window into extreme physics, but detection requires next-generation detectors and coordinated electromagnetic follow-up.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is probed by neutron star properties.
method: Review of gravitational-wave signals from binary neutron star mergers and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are presented and compared to theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined approaches.
result: The review highlights how these techniques can directly image disorder and defects at the atomic scale.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more complete picture of atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonances.
motivation: Understanding nuclear reactions in stars is crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many reactions are difficult to measure directly.
method: Summarizes theoretical approaches for low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects.
result: Provides an overview of the state of the art in theoretical nuclear astrophysics and new ideas for laboratory studies.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical phenomena dominate low-energy stellar reactions, and further theoretical and experimental work is needed.

motivation: To provide a self-consistent set of fundamental constants for use in physics and chemistry.
method: Least-squares adjustment of all available data up to end of 2022.
result: Updated values for constants such as Planck constant, elementary charge, etc.
conclusion: The new recommended values supersede previous CODATA sets and are the standard reference.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions used in electronic-structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, describing how Wannier functions are constructed and applied.
result: It catalogs the ecosystem of Wannier-function software and highlights its applications in materials science.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for understanding and designing materials.

motivation: Perovskite solar cells suffer from thermal cycling instability due to grain boundary defects; the authors aim to enhance durability and efficiency.
method: They introduce a wide-temperature-range fluid-phase molecular complex that forms dynamically adaptive grain boundaries in perovskite films.
result: The approach achieves an efficiency of 26.52% and improved thermal cycling stability.
conclusion: Fluid-phase grain boundaries offer a promising route to temperature-robust perovskite solar cells.

method: Seven scientists provide their perspectives on how they use AFM and their hopes for its future.
result: The article presents a collection of viewpoints rather than new experimental or theoretical results.
conclusion: AFM remains a versatile and essential tool, with ongoing developments expected to expand its capabilities.

authors: Aurelien David

abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 17 June 2026;
tldr: A review of the physics of GaN-based LEDs, focusing on polarization fields, carrier localization, and non-radiative defects.
motivation: GaN-based LEDs are crucial for modern lighting, but their efficiency is governed by complex physical effects that need to be understood.
method: The review synthesizes existing research on polarization fields, carrier localization, and non-radiative defects in GaN LEDs.
result: The paper describes how these three effects impact LED performance, including efficiency droop and emission wavelength.
conclusion: Understanding these physical mechanisms is key to further improving GaN LED efficiency and light output.

motivation: To understand how structural variation and repetitive elements influence recombination in wild tomatoes, which could inform breeding strategies for modern tomatoes.
method: The authors sequenced and assembled genomes of multiple wild tomato species, then performed comparative genomics to identify structural variants and repeat content, correlating them with recombination patterns.
result: Structural variants and repeat content were found to act as barriers to meiotic recombination, affecting the distribution of crossovers.
conclusion: These findings provide insights into the genomic factors that shape recombination landscapes in tomatoes, with implications for crop improvement.

method: Design hyperbranched networks to expand inter-chain spacing and suppress secondary relaxation.
result: Achieved 4.9 J/cm³ energy density with 90% efficiency at 250°C.
conclusion: Hyperbranched network design is effective for high-temperature capacitive energy storage.

authors: Dirk W. Beck
Alexander Friedman
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 27 June 2026;
tldr: This paper proposes that dopamine signals in the brain track information gain about action selection, unifying learning, movement, and decision-making.
motivation: To explain how dopamine and striosome circuits coordinate diverse functions like learning, movement, and decision-making under a single principle.
method: The authors develop a computational model where dopamine encodes the information gain from new information about which action to take, and test it against neural data.
result: Dopamine signals correlate with prediction error defined as information gain, not reward prediction error, unifying its roles.
conclusion: Dopamine's diverse functions can be understood as tracking information gain, providing a unified framework for striosome-dopamine circuit function.
